lines.text: The phrase "unworthy servants" means the same as
"wretched"; it does not mean servants who do their duty
badly so that when we have only half fulfilled or not fulfilled
at all our obligations, God is a terrifying master for us. The
parable is not speaking for example of God as our Judge,
before whom we stand as imperfect, impure, and sinful men.
It is speaking about God as Lord, before whom we stand
forth as miserable creatures, even when we have done all that
was commanded us. In that this is so, it speaks a message
of comfort just to those who suffer from the consciousness of
their imperfection. God does not consider whether you are
more or less perfect! In His sight no one is better than another,
if perfection is the standard: "When you have done all that
is commanded you, say, 'We are unworthy servants!' " This
is what Luther means when he sings:
" 'Tis through Thy love alone we gain
The pardon of our sin;
The strictest life is but in vain,
Our works can nothing win;
That none should boast himself of aught,
But own in fear Thy grace hath wrought
What in him seemeth righteous."1
Have we now some idea what our parable wishes to teach
us, and in what way it is a message of divine grace? It is a
comforting word of grace because it teaches us that we
wretched human beings cannot live otherwise than by the
inspiration of God's grace. It teaches us this, precisely
because it shows us God as He really is, as our Lord, before
whom we poor mortals can have no right, can raise no claim.
It is a liberating and saving word because it frees us from the
illusion that we might, because of what we are and achieve,
lay claim to some justification in the sight of God. Only he
who surrenders all presumption to right and claim before
God, only he can live by God's grace.
This, however, seems a hard thing for man—to renounce
every right in the eyes of God and to silence every claim, to
cast himself utterly and unconditionally on divine favour
1 Tr. Catherine Winkworth.
